text:
I


If they tell you I am growing old

because reading tires me

or the pen wearies me, or I have had enough

of philosophies I do not understand;


if another judges that I collect the dividend

from an invested treasure, and claims

that I live on my own sinecure

and depend only on my habits,


send them to the new spring

that must bring forth shoots, so that

they may forget yesterday's fruits;


but if you know that I closed my eyes

to the challenge of red lips,

then you may count me lost.


II


Without forgetting for a moment

the patience and resignation of the gardener,

at every hour I apply the diligence

my daily commerce requires.


Since I have never felt the difference

between what I lose and what I gain,

I sow without slackness or fervor

in the furrow traced by my hand.


While the appointed hour arrives,

I guard the bud, tend the graft,

raise the stem of the beloved flower,


pull the weeds from my garden,

and when I loosen my fist from the hoe

you will pronounce me dead without asking.

translation.title: The Ominous Sign
translation.editorial_note: The two sonnet-like sections preserve the poem’s shift from rumors of aging to the gardening metaphor of desire and death.
